Jury briefing · 31 October 2026

PULSE

Hypertension monitoring, early warning and emergency support for Algerian patients and their doctors.

A 36-hour hackathon prototype by a team of three: backend + integration (Ayoub), frontend, and data + AI/ML (me). This page explains the whole project, what I built, what every data field and every AI model is for, and the questions the jury (including the doctor) is likely to ask.

24database tables, access rules on every one
6AI models built, tested, documented
4real public datasets used to calibrate and check
17–20 minearly warning before a ring limit is crossed (simulated nights)
Prototype, not a medical device. All patient data is fictional and labelled simulated. Real public datasets were used only as statistics, to make the simulator realistic and to check the rules.
01 · Script

The 5-minute pitch (read it out loud)

  1. Problem (30 s). "In Algeria about one adult in three has high blood pressure, and 41 % of them don't know it. Those who know are followed with a few doctor visits a year. Between visits, nobody sees the numbers, and a hypertensive crisis can arrive alone at home."
  2. What PULSE is (30 s). "PULSE connects the patient at home to their own doctor. The patient records blood-pressure readings and symptoms, or sends data from a cuff or a bracelet. Fixed medical rules react immediately. The doctor sees everything in one dashboard, plus AI help to see problems earlier."
  3. Safety first (30 s). "Alerts come only from fixed rules reviewed by our medical mentor: 180/120, red-flag symptoms, low pressure. The AI never raises an alarm, never diagnoses, never touches medication, and the patient never sees AI output. It only informs the doctor."
  4. The AI (90 s). "My part: the data and the AI. One secure database with 24 tables. Six small, explainable models: tomorrow morning's blood pressure, a nightly check of the bracelet, a weekly report for the doctor, and a live engine that warns the doctor about 17 to 20 minutes before oxygen or heart rate crosses a limit, on simulated nights. Every model was compared with a simple method on patients it had never seen."
  5. Honesty (30 s). "No open dataset has daily home blood pressure for many patients, so we trained on a simulator calibrated on a real home series, and checked our oxygen rule on real sleep-lab nights. One model trained on 2,309 real people was too weak, so we hid it from doctors."
  6. Demo (60 s). Patient Nadia enters 186/118 → alarm and symptom check. Doctor opens Karim → bracelet signals, early warning, tomorrow's estimate, weekly report.
  7. Close (15 s). "Next: a validated cuff, consented real data, and re-testing every model on real patients. The rules are already clinician-reviewed."
02 · Why

The problem in Algeria

National WHO STEPS survey 2016–2017, 6,765 adults aged 18–69 (Moussouni et al., BMC Public Health 2022):

31.6 %have hypertension (women 34.2 %, men 28.3 %)
36.2 %are pre-hypertensive
41.1 %of hypertensive people didn't know
67.8 %abdominal obesity; 24.9 % obesity

Independent risk factors found: age (60–69 vs 18–29, odds ratio 12.3), high cholesterol (2.0), obesity BMI ≥ 30 (1.7), abdominal obesity (1.7). Bread is a major salt source (a bakery pilot found about 17 g of salt per kg of bread, so roughly 8–9 g a day from bread alone, while WHO recommends under 5 g a day in total).

What goes wrong today

  • Home readings are written on paper or not at all; the doctor sees them months later, if ever.
  • Patients don't know which number is dangerous, or what to do when it is.
  • No early signal between visits: the doctor learns about a bad month at the next appointment.
"PULSE closes the gap between visits: the patient knows what to do with each reading, and the doctor sees the trend before it becomes an emergency."
03 · What

The solution: three users, one record

Patient

  • Enters a reading (or imports a CSV / syncs a device)
  • Gets an immediate, plain explanation and next step
  • Symptom check; emergency screen with call button (14, Protection civile), medical card, trusted contact
  • Alarm that rings for a crisis until the patient confirms with the password
  • History, alerts, journal (food, activity), profile

Doctor

  • List of assigned patients, sorted by urgency (emergency > severe > trend > notice)
  • Patient record: readings, alerts, incidents, journal, notes, care plan (BP target)
  • AI panels: tomorrow's estimate, bracelet signals and early warnings, weekly report, personal ranges to approve
  • Reviews and resolves alerts

Admin

  • Creates doctor roles
  • Assigns patients to doctors (this drives all doctor access)
  • Reads the audit log (who changed what)

Interface in French, emergency screen French + Arabic, timezone Africa/Algiers by default.

06 · Database

One secure database for patients, doctors and AI

GroupTablesWhat they hold
People & accessprofiles, patient_profiles, doctor_patient_assignments, body_measurements, audit_logAccounts and roles, medical background and risk factors, who follows whom, weight/height/waist, change history.
Readings & devicesmeasurements, devices, ingestion_batches, wearable_samplesEvery BP reading (append-only), devices, each import (with a file fingerprint), ring/bracelet samples.
Daily lifesymptom_reports, lifestyle_logs, medications, medication_adherence_events, journal_entriesSymptoms, meals/activity/sleep/stress/fasting, prescriptions and doses taken/missed, notes for the doctor.
Carecare_plans, doctor_notes, alerts, alert_measurementsDoctor's BP target and plan, private notes, rule alerts and the readings in each alert episode.
Emergencytrusted_contacts, emergency_eventsPeople to call; emergency screen history (actions logged as "tapped", never "called").
AI outputsml_predictions, wearable_flags, patient_bands, weekly_reportsEstimates, ring flags and early warnings, personal ranges, weekly reports. Doctor and admin only.

Security and quality, enforced by the database itself

  • Row-level security on all 24 tables; nothing for logged-out users; public sign-up turned off.
  • A doctor sees only patients actively assigned to them.
  • Patients can't read any AI output (database rule, not just hidden in the UI).
  • Readings can't be edited or deleted by app users: a wrong entry stays, flagged.
  • Simulated data must be labelled simulated, or the database rejects it.
  • Same file can never be imported twice (SHA-256 fingerprint).
  • Data minimisation: birth year only, no full date of birth; location only with consent.
  • Audit log on profiles, assignments, care plans, notes, medications, alerts.

Built in 9 steps (migrations), all in the cloud

#MigrationAdds
M1core_schemaAll core tables, validation trigger, audit log
M2access_policiesRow-level security policies for each role
M3backend_alignmentAlert episodes, "rested 5 min", symptom "none of these", backend fields
M4ml_predictionsNext-day BP estimates table (doctor only)
M5patient_birth_yearAge (year only)
M6algerian_factors_wearablesSex, smoking, coded conditions, salt/bread habits, weight/waist, fasting days, language, ring samples

07 · Logic

The life of one blood-pressure reading

1 · EnterPatient types it, imports a CSV, or a device syncs
→
2 · FormatAPI/importer checks numbers, unit mmHg, time
→
3 · ValidateDatabase trigger: valid / needs review / invalid + reasons
→
4 · RulesFixed rules on the reading + symptoms
→
5 · AlertNew alert or attached to the open episode
→
6 · PatientNext step; alarm and emergency screen if needed
→
7 · DoctorList sorted by urgency; review, resolve
→
8 · AINext jobs use valid readings only, for the doctor

Validation policy pulse-v1 (runs on every reading, from every path)

ResultRuleWhy
invalidsystolic ≤ diastolic · systolic outside 50–300 · diastolic outside 25–200 · pulse outside 25–250 · time more than 5 min in the futureNot a possible human value: a typo or device fault. Stored for traceability, never averaged, never used by AI.
needs reviewsystolic outside 70–250 or diastolic outside 40–150 · estimated (not a cuff) · same values within 2 min (double entry) · device reported a problem (movement, cuff fit, irregular pulse, position)Possible but suspicious. Kept and shown with its reason. Still goes through the alert rules, so a real crisis is never hidden.
valideverything elseA very high reading like 186/118 is valid data: it is an alert matter, not a data problem.

Missing data is never filled in: a missing reading means "not recorded", never "normal".

08 · Safety path

Alert rules: fixed, medical, no AI

These rules live in the backend (api/app/analysis/rules.py). They are deterministic: the same reading always gives the same answer. Thresholds were reviewed by the team's medical mentor on 30 October 2026.

RuleWhenLevelWhat happens
R-EMG-1Any red-flag symptom (chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, weakness, numbness, vision change, difficulty speaking)emergencyEmergency screen immediately, whatever the reading. Call button (14).
R-SEV-1Systolic ≥ 180 or diastolic ≥ 120severeAlarm, symptom check, recheck after 60 seconds.
R-SEV-2Recheck within 15 min still ≥ 180 / 120severe, persistentAttached to the same episode; urgent guidance.
R-SEV-3Recheck within 15 min below 180 / 120severeAlert stays open for the doctor; reading attached.
R-TGT-1Reading ≥ the doctor's target (default 140/90)noticeOne active notice per patient.
R-LOW-2Systolic < 70lowSymptom check and recheck after 60 s (proposed, D27).
R-LOW-1Systolic < 90 or diastolic < 60lowOne active low alert per patient (proposed, D27).
R-TRD-1≥ 3 valid readings in 7 days with a mean ≥ targettrendOne active trend alert per patient. Simulated readings never count.

Alert states: open → acknowledged (patient confirms with password, or doctor) → reviewed → resolved (doctor; a note is required for severe and emergency).

180/120 is the ACC/AHA "hypertensive crisis" level. The 60-second recheck follows the usual advice to confirm a very high value with a second measurement. The red-flag list is the AHA list of signs of target-organ damage. 140/90 is the default target only until the doctor sets a care plan; the home-BP alternative 135/85 is used in the weekly report categories. Low-pressure thresholds (90/60, 70) are proposed and waiting for clinician sign-off.
09 · Every factor

Every data factor: why it exists and how it's used

Each field in the database has a reason. The reasons come from the Algerian STEPS survey, international guidelines, and what a doctor needs to read the numbers correctly.

Used by: Rules fixed alerts · AI a model input or adjustment · Doctor shown for clinical context · Quality data quality

C. Chronic conditions that change how the bracelet is read

ConditionEffect in PULSEEvidence
COPDSpO2 limit moves from 94 % to 88 %; the doctor confirms by approving the patient's range.BTS 2017 oxygen guideline: target 88–92 % for patients at risk of hypercapnic failure.
Atrial fibrillationHRV (RMSSD) and the multi-signal anomaly score are ignored.Beat-to-beat intervals are irregular, so HRV says nothing about stress or recovery.
Obstructive sleep apneaExpected night oxygen dips; the doctor sees them as ring flags.OSA in 83.5 % of resistant-hypertension patients (multicenter cohort, 284 patients).
Asthma, heart failure, thyroid diseaseRecorded as context for the doctor and the risk model.Can change heart rate, breathing and BP readings.
"Every field exists for a reason. Age, waist, cholesterol and obesity are the factors the Algerian national survey found significant. We ask about bread because it's the main source of salt here and patients don't count milligrams. And chronic conditions change the rules: for a COPD patient, 89 % oxygen is not the same signal as for anyone else."
10 · Symptoms

Symptoms: why each one is there

Symptoms are checked independently of the reading: a red-flag symptom opens the emergency path even if the blood pressure is normal.

SymptomRed flag?What it can signal (why a doctor cares)
Chest painyesHeart damage (acute coronary syndrome) or aortic dissection
Back painyesAortic dissection
Shortness of breathyesAcute heart failure / fluid in the lungs
Weakness, numbnessyesStroke
Difficulty speakingyesStroke
Vision changeyesStroke, damage to the retina, hypertensive encephalopathy
Severe headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, palpitations, otherrecordedShown to the doctor and asked in the symptom check; not an emergency on their own in this version (AHA list of 7). The doctor can change this list.
"None of these"—An explicit "no symptoms" answer, different from "not asked".
11 · Bracelet / ring

Ring and bracelet signals: what each one tells us

SignalPopulation limitPersonal checkWhy we use it
Heart rate (bpm)> 100 at rest (Mayo Clinic: 60–100). Only "too high" is flagged: fit people can be below 60.Own 28-night normalA rising night heart rate can signal illness, stress, poor sleep or a heart problem.
HRV (RMSSD, ms)None (too personal)Own normal only; ignored with atrial fibrillationA drop in HRV signals stress, illness or poor recovery.
SpO2 (oxygen, %)< 94 % (BTS); < 88 % with COPDOwn normalNight oxygen dips are a sign of sleep apnea, which is linked to resistant hypertension.
Skin temperature (°C)NoneOwn night normal + 1.0 °CThe start of a fever.
What a bracelet is NOT used for: blood pressure. Cuffless BP estimates are not recommended for diagnosing or managing hypertension (European Society of Hypertension, 2022). In PULSE a bracelet estimate is always labelled "estimate", is "needs review", and is left out of averages and AI training. Ring data never triggers an alert: it goes to the doctor as advisory flags. Consumer SpO2 is less accurate than a clinical oximeter and can overestimate in darker skin (FDA, 2021).
12 · Data

Simulated where no real data exists, real where it does

Simulated (always labelled)

  • 12 demo patients with stories: Karim (sleep apnea), Fatima (COPD), Houria (atrial fibrillation), rising BP… Risk factors of 8 of them drawn from the STEPS percentages.
  • Training cohort: 200 patients × 90 days.
  • Unseen test cohort: 100 new patients, used only for the 30-day test.
  • Ring data: built from published values (normal ranges, apnea, COPD); 20,832 samples in the cloud demo (12 patients × 28 nights).
  • Live nights: 700 + 700 minute-by-minute nights with situations: oxygen falling, heart rate climbing, fever, restless sleep, loose ring, bathroom trip, apnea.

Real public data (statistics only, never uploaded)

DatasetUsed for
NHANES 2017–2020 (CDC, US)Pulse/BP percentiles by age and sex; risk model training (2,309 treated adults)
NHANES 2021–2023External test on new real people (1,851)
Mendeley home BP (1 patient, 128 readings)Made the simulator realistic
PhysioNet Apnea-ECG (8 nights)Checked the ring oxygen rule

How the simulator was made realistic

The first simulator was too smooth: blood pressure varied about half as much as in real life, so the model looked better than it was (error 5.2 mmHg). We calibrated version 2 on the real home series:

Systolic, measured every 3 daysSpread (SD)Typical changeCorrelation
Real home series11.710.00.40
Simulator v2 (used)11.810.00.41
Simulator v1 (dropped)6.76.50.24
"No open dataset has daily home blood pressure for many patients. So we built a simulator, matched its day-to-day variation to a real home series, and retrained. The error went up from 5.2 to 7.8 mmHg, and that's the honest number."
13 · The AI

What the AI does, and when

WhenJobReadsWrites (doctor only)
Every dayNext-day BP estimate (mbp-v1.1)Valid readings of the last 7 daysEstimate + 90 % range for tomorrow morning, or "not enough history"
Every nightRing night monitor (ring-v1.1)Night medians 00:00–06:00 of HR, HRV, SpO2, temperatureFlags: outside medical limits, outside own normal, unusual pattern
Every minuteLive early warning (live-v1)Last 60 minutes of ring samplesEarly warning: "limit likely crossed within 20 min"; "night going badly"
Every weekWeekly report (wcls-v1.1 + summaries)The week's readings, ring flags, target, age/sexReport: home-BP category, control vs target, chance next week is above target, pulse vs same age/sex; proposed personal ranges
When the doctor reviewsFeedback loopConfirmed / dismissed flags, approved rangesPersonal thresholds retuned; a new version must still find the known events; never deployed automatically
The rule we never break: the AI only informs the doctor. It never raises an alarm, never diagnoses, never touches medication, and patients see no AI output (enforced in the database). If every AI job is off, the alerts and the emergency screen still work.
14 · Models

Six models, each answering one question

ModelQuestionMethodStatus
mbp-v1.1What will tomorrow morning's BP be?Ridge regression + 90 % range (split-conformal)served
ring-v1.1Was tonight unusual for this patient?Medical limits + own 28-night normal (robust z > 3.5) + IsolationForestserved (flags)
wcls-v1.1Will next week be above the BP target?Logistic regressionweekly report
live-v1Will a limit be crossed in the next 20 minutes?Gradient boosting, checked every new minutebuilt, not switched on
mbp-v2.1Does ring data improve the BP estimate?mbp + ring featuresexperiment: no gain
wrisk-v1Is BP uncontrolled despite treatment?Trained on 2,309 real people (NHANES)hidden: too weak
mbp-v1.1 — the inputs (21 features) and what each one means
FeatureMeaningWhy
Last morning sys/diaMost recent morning readingStrongest short-term signal
7-day and 3-day meansAverage of the last week / 3 daysSmooth out single noisy readings
7-day morning meanMornings onlyTarget is a morning value
Slope (7 days)Is BP going up or down?Captures a trend
Spread (SD)How variable the patient isVariable patients are less predictable
Morning − evening gapDifference between morning and evening readingsMorning surge pattern
Number of readings, days with a readingData coverageLess data = less certain
Day of week (7)Monday … SundayWeekly routine effects

Eligibility: ≥ 6 valid readings on ≥ 4 days in the last 7 days, with ≥ 1 morning reading; otherwise "insufficient history" (never a guess). Why ridge: chosen on validation over gradient boosting (6.18 vs 6.30 mmHg) and fully explainable. Shown as: "Model estimate (synthetic training data)".

ring-v1.1 — three checks each night
  1. Medical limits: SpO2 < 94 % (COPD 88 %), resting heart rate > 100.
  2. Own normal: robust z-score > 3.5 against the patient's last 28 nights, or outside the doctor-approved range. z = 3.5 was chosen on validation patients: 2.5 gave almost one false flag per patient every week; 3.5 gave 0.22.
  3. IsolationForest: an anomaly detector that looks at all signals together.

Uses the night median, not the minimum: on real sleep-lab data, even healthy people's minimum reached 57–69 % from sensor artefacts.

wcls-v1.1 — the weekly classifier

Inputs: the week's mean systolic/diastolic, number of readings, morning and evening means, slope, spread, last 3 readings, distance to target. Label: next week's home mean ≥ target. Ring features were tried and didn't help (0.956 vs 0.959 AUROC on validation).

live-v1 — the live engine's inputs
FeatureMeaning
d15, d30Current value (3-minute median) minus the median of the last 15 / 30 minutes
slope10, slope25Speed of change over 10 / 25 minutes
sd15Variability over 15 minutes
devDistance from the patient's personal night normal
marginDistance to the limit (still inside = positive)
Restless night: awake share, bouts, HR excess, HRV ratio, time elapsedHow much of the night the heart rate was ≥ 10 bpm above sleeping normal, for 3+ minutes

The 3-minute median means one loose-ring reading can't trigger anything. A warning needs 2 minutes in a row, then 30 minutes of quiet per patient and signal. No warning if the newest sample is older than 2 minutes. A first linear version learned "it always comes back to normal" and never warned, so we replaced it with gradient boosting.

wrisk-v1 — trained on real people, then hidden

Inputs: only fields PULSE has — age, sex, BMI, waist, smoking, diabetes, cholesterol, kidney disease, COPD, heart failure, stroke. Survey-weighted. External test AUROC 0.596 vs 0.565 for age + sex alone. A near-random score would mislead a doctor, so it is not displayed.

30-day test on 100 patients no model had seen

Each test day (2–31 March), the frozen model saw only earlier days, exactly as in real use.

Next-morning systolic error (mean absolute, mmHg; lower is better), 2,271 patient-days

"Same as yesterday"
9.50

  • Diastolic error 4.56 mmHg (7-day mean 4.83). 68.6 % of estimates within 10 mmHg.
  • The 90 % range contained the true value 90.7 % of the time (it's honest about its uncertainty).

Other flags per patient-week: limits only 1.12 (mostly real low oxygen in apnea patients), IsolationForest 0.08, personal normal 0.22. Real check: the oxygen rule flagged 4 / 4 real sleep-apnea nights and 0 / 3 healthy nights (PhysioNet).

Honest limit: it ranks patients well but can't predict the weeks where the status changes. So it's shown as "how close to the target line", not as a forecast of change.
16 · Live early warning

Warns the doctor 17–20 minutes before a limit is crossed

SIMULATOR-ONLY RESULTS: 700 + 700 simulated nights. This shows the mechanism works; it is not real-world or clinical validation.

One unseen simulated night with falling oxygen, replayed minute by minute (SpO2 %, 3-minute median; illustrative redraw). Warned 17 min before the limit, 29 min before the old rule.

Situation (unseen simulated nights)Warned before the limitHow early (median)Old "limit crossed now" rule
Oxygen falling93.5 %~17 min before7 min after
Heart rate climbing97.1 %~20 min before9 min after
Fever starting94.5 %~17 min before(no rule)
  • False warnings: about 1 in 25 normal nights (0.04 per night); 0.03 with a loose ring or bathroom spike.
  • Restless nights: 94.9 % warned, typically by 01:00 (AUROC 0.966 at 01:00).
  • Speed: about 44 ms per new minute per patient.
Settings reviewed and accepted by the medical mentor on 30 October 2026: SpO2 trigger 94 % (COPD 88 %), sleeping HR limit 100 bpm, temperature personal + 1.0 °C, warning thresholds HR 0.35 / SpO2 0.45 / temperature 0.85, 20-min horizon, 2 minutes in a row, 30-min quiet period, 2-min freshness, restless night P ≥ 0.7. The review covers the settings, not the results.
17 · Doctor in charge

The weekly doctor loop

1 · Nights checkedRing flags written for the doctor
→
2 · Weekly reportHome-BP category, control vs target, chance next week is above target, pulse vs same age/sex
→
3 · Model proposesA personal range per ring signal
→
4 · Doctor decidesApproves, edits or rejects; next nights are judged against the doctor's range

Home-BP categories use the ACC/AHA 2017 home values (home 135/85 = office 140/90), never office grades on home readings. Doctor-reviewed flags become labels; a retuned version must still find the known events, and nothing is deployed automatically.

18 · Safety by design

Designed so the AI never acts on its own

  • Advisory only: AI output goes to the doctor, never to the patient (enforced in the database).
  • Fixed rules decide alerts in the backend; symptoms open the emergency path on their own.
  • Emergency number 14 (Protection civile); never dialled in tests or in the demo.
  • No medication advice, no diagnosis, anywhere.
  • Every simulated row is labelled; real datasets used only as statistics, under their licences.
  • Every model has a model card: data, method, results, limits.
  • Honest logging: "call button tapped", never "call made".
  • Nothing silently deleted: wrong readings stay, flagged; health values never in logs.
Clinician review done (30 Oct): alert thresholds 180/120, red-flag list, SpO2 94 % (COPD 88 %), personal-range rule, patient wording, every live-v1 setting, ring personal limit z 3.5, proposed ring rule R-RING-1. Still awaiting sign-off: low-pressure thresholds (D27) and the alarm behaviour (D29).
19 · Honesty

What is and isn't validated

ClaimEvidence
Simulator realismMatched to a real home-BP series
Ring oxygen rule8 real sleep-lab nights (4/4 apnea, 0/3 healthy) — sleep-lab oximeter, not a ring
Next-day BP, weekly classifierUnseen simulated patients only
Live early warningSimulated nights only
Risk factors predicting control (wrisk-v1)Real people: too weak (0.596), so hidden
"When a model was too weak on real people, we hid it. The lesson: risk factors can't tell whose blood pressure is controlled. Control has to be measured, and that's exactly what PULSE does."
20 · Demo

Demo script and screenshots

  1. Patient Nadia (no ring) → dashboard → enter 186/118 → the alarm rings, symptom check, recheck in 60 s → confirm with the password.
  2. Enter 80/50 → low-pressure notice. Enter 1/1/1 → invalid, symptom check (never silently "saved").
  3. Import a CSV → readings go through the same rules; a simulated file only previews.
  4. Doctor → patient list sorted by urgency → Karim (sleep apnea, simulated ring) → alerts, bracelet signals, live early warning, tomorrow's estimate, weekly report, approve a personal range.
  5. Optional live: start the minute-by-minute stream for Karim with "oxygen falling" → an early warning appears before the "limit crossed" flag.

Accounts: patient.a (Nadia), patient.b (Karim), medecin. Passwords in .dev/demo-credentials.txt. Full steps: docs/data/DEMO_RUNBOOK.pdf.

21 · Real hardware

Real bracelet bridge (Bluetooth)

Any bracelet with the standard Bluetooth Heart Rate service (0x180D) — e.g. Polar Verity Sense (~€89) or a Coospo armband (~€25) — can stream real heart rate (every 5 s) and HRV (every 5 min, when the device sends beat intervals) into the database, labelled device_sync.

  • Research result: affordable devices can stream only heart rate and HRV live. SpO2, temperature and BP can't be streamed on a standard profile.
  • An HR-only early warning needs about 29 minutes of data, so on stage we use Karim's simulated "oxygen falling" stream.
  • Built and ready on the local stack; not yet run with real hardware.
  • For blood pressure itself we recommend a validated upper-arm cuff (Bluetooth Blood Pressure Profile 0x1810); the database already accepts its readings and quality flags.

23 · Questions

Likely jury questions, short answers

QuestionAnswer
Is this real patient data?No. All patient data is simulated and labelled. Real public data was used to make the simulator realistic and to check the rules.
How accurate is it?On 100 unseen simulated patients, next-day systolic error is 7.9 mmHg, better than simple methods on every one of 30 days. Real accuracy needs consented PULSE data.
Can the AI raise an alarm?No. Alerts come from fixed medical rules. The AI only informs the doctor; patients never see it.
Why not deep learning?Little data, and doctors need to understand the output. Small models beat simple baselines and are easy to explain.
You have no ring. How do you know it works?Ring data is simulated from published values; the oxygen rule was checked on 8 real sleep-lab nights (4/4 apnea flagged, 0/3 healthy). And the Bluetooth bridge already takes real heart rate from a bracelet.
Did any model fail?Yes: the real-data risk model (AUROC 0.60) was too weak, so we hid it. A first live forecaster never warned; we replaced it.
What about privacy?Row-level security in the database, doctors see only assigned patients, birth year only, location only with consent, audit log, no health values in logs, public sign-up off.
What if the internet is down?The emergency config and medical card are cached on the device, so the emergency screen still shows the number to call.
Does PULSE call the ambulance?No automated channel to the Protection civile exists; the patient presses the call button (14). We log "tapped", never "called".
Business model / who pays?Prototype stage. Natural paths: clinics and cardiologists following hypertensive patients, insurers (CNAS/CASNOS), or a pharmacy partnership for validated cuffs. (Adapt to the team's pitch.)
Why Supabase?Real PostgreSQL with access rules enforced by the database itself, built-in login, hosted in Paris close to Algeria.
What did you do?The whole data and AI part: database design and security, data quality, import tools, simulator, real-data calibration, the six models, their evaluation, and the doctor-side AI panels' data.
24 · Doctor questions

Questions the doctor on the jury may ask

QuestionAnswer
Why 180/120?ACC/AHA hypertensive-crisis threshold. Reviewed by our medical mentor. A recheck after 60 s confirms or not.
Why a default target of 140/90 for home readings? Home should be 135/85.Correct. 140/90 is only a placeholder until the doctor sets the care plan (decision D2, open to change). The weekly report already uses the home categories (135/85 = office 140/90, ACC/AHA Table 11).
Why aren't severe headache or confusion red flags?We used the AHA list of 7 for this version; they are recorded and asked in the symptom check. Adding them is a one-line change we'd make on clinical advice.
How do you handle measurement technique?We record rest 5 min, position and arm; device flags (movement, cuff fit, irregular pulse) make a reading "needs review"; double entries within 2 minutes are flagged.
Why not use the smartwatch BP?ESH 2022: cuffless devices aren't recommended for diagnosis or management. Estimates are labelled and excluded from averages and AI.
COPD patients will always be "low" on oxygen.Their limit is 88 % (BTS 2017), and the doctor confirms by approving the patient's range.
HRV with atrial fibrillation?Ignored: irregular beats make RMSSD meaningless.
Consumer SpO2 accuracy?Less accurate than a clinical oximeter, can overestimate in darker skin (FDA 2021). That's why we use the night median, and why ring data is advisory only.
Ramadan?Fasting days are logged (start → iftar); medication timing remains the doctor's decision. Studies show BP mostly stable when treatment continues.
Does PULSE give medication advice?Never. Doses are stored as the doctor wrote them; PULSE never computes or changes them.
Low blood pressure?Proposed rules: < 90/60 low notice; systolic < 70 symptom check and recheck. Awaiting your kind of sign-off.
Would you trust the next-day estimate?Not for decisions: it's labelled "model estimate (synthetic training data)" and shown with its 90 % range. It's for seeing a direction early, not for treatment.
25 · Words

Glossary (to explain terms simply)

TermPlain meaning
MAEMean absolute error: on average, how many mmHg the estimate is off.
AUROCHow well a model ranks cases: 0.5 = coin flip, 1.0 = perfect.
Brier scoreHow good the probabilities are: lower is better.
BaselineA simple method ("same as yesterday") a model must beat to be worth it.
BacktestReplaying past days one by one, letting the model see only earlier data.
Ridge regressionA linear formula with a penalty that prevents over-fitting; easy to explain.
Logistic regressionA linear model that outputs a probability (yes/no question).
Gradient boostingMany small decision trees added together; good at non-linear patterns.
IsolationForestAn anomaly detector: points that are easy to "isolate" are unusual.
Robust z-scoreHow far tonight is from the patient's usual, in units of their usual variation (using median, not mean).
Split-conformal rangeA range built so that it contains the true value a chosen share of the time (90 %).
RMSSD (HRV)Heart-rate variability: variation between consecutive beats.
SpO2Blood oxygen saturation, in %.
ODI-4Number of oxygen drops of ≥ 4 % per hour of sleep.
Row-level security (RLS)The database decides, row by row, who may read or write.
MigrationA numbered, versioned change to the database structure.
Synthetic / simulatedGenerated data, not from a real person; always labelled.
